  B.  Malibu Schools Centralized Fundraising & Athletics Pathways
  Recommended Action: Provide a recommendation to the City Council regarding a
  Special Funding Request for Malibu Centralized Fundraising & Athletics
  Pathways.

  Assistant City Manager Toney provided background information on the item and
  introduced Karin Al-Hardan from the Malibu Schools Leadership Council 2023 to
  provide a presentation.

  Ms. Al-Hardan provided a presentation on the Malibu Centralized Fundraising and
  Athletics Pathway fund request. She went over the goals of the project, current state
  of the fundraising program, recommendations, timelines, and budget. She
  explained that the reason for the monetary request from the City of Malibu is due
  to preparation efforts for the district separation, to serve young members beginning
  at the elementary level, and to provide athletic support for all. A three-year plan
  was presented along with a benchmark report and fundraising goals, which
  reflected the need for a consultant, executive director, and other operational
  resources.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart opened the floor for public comment. At this time, there
  were no members of the public in this meeting.

  Councilmember Silverstein asked a clarifying question whether the money was for
  an entity creation or for actual programing for the schools and asked what the
  projected fundraising levels will be over the next 3-5 years once established.

  Ms. Al-Hardan explained that it would primarily be to create an entity with the
  guidance of a consultant and that the athletic pathway portion is funding the actual
  schools. She estimated a goal of offsetting half of the cost by the first year and full
  cost by the second year with the goal of establishing endowments, an alumni
  program, and pursuing corporate donations.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart commended everyone who worked on this request. He
  inquired about the possibility of using the library fund. He also asked for
  clarification on exactly how much they are requesting, and if it was annual or total
  over two years.

  Ms. Al-Hardan provided an update on the library fund request, stating that she has
  not heard back from the library team. She reviewed the budget attachment and
  clarified that they are requesting closer to half a million dollars each year and

  explained the columns where the City of Malibu money would fit versus the funds
  provided by the Santa Monica Malibu School District, reviewing both a break down
  of centralized funding and an athletic program.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart requested to hear more about benchmarks and more about
  the breakdown between the centralized fundraising entity funding and the athletics
  pathway funding. He emphasized that these funds are meant to be temporary seed
  money and after time less funds would be needed from the city. He also inquired
  what the total amount needed from the city would be.

  Ms. Al-Hardan explained that the school district was unable to provide all requested
  funds and explained the budget attachment breakdown and where the city funds
  would be allocated to. She stated that once the entity is self-funding, they would
  stop requesting city funds and added that they have a three-year goal. She added
  that the total amount requested from the city over the years would be $2,085,500.

  Councilmember Silverstein requested more information regarding how
  benchmarks would be measured and what would constitute success. He inquired
  about the ratio between what is being spent and what would be fundraised.

  Ms. Al-Hardan explained that currently benchmarks have not been established and
  goals are based on hiring the needed staff to carry out this project. She added that
  with a consultant they would be able to have a better understanding of what the
  benchmarks would be within three months. She also explained that there would be
  a goal of establishing a three-million-dollar endowment similar to the model of the
  Santa Monica Education Foundation (SMEF).

  Councilmember Silverstein requested more information on how SMEF was
  funding their entity, how it was initially funded, and what their operating budget is.
  He inquired if there were any efforts to get seen money from the community.

  Ms. Al-Hardan elaborated that SMEF was funded the same way, with an 80/20
  model where 80% goes to the endowment and 20% goes to the schools. She added
  that they are currently self-funded from an initial seed money that came from the
  City of Santa Monica. She did not have the budget information along with the total
  amount of seed money provided by Santa Monica readily available and said she
  would provide it at a later date. She stated that there have been no efforts to get this
  seed money from the community because it is a lot of money to request from
  parents.

  Councilmember Silverstein proposed providing the initial funding for the next six
  months to cover a consultant in order to get more details about the benchmarks and
  plans.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart clarified that the request is close to $500,000 each year for
  three years and recommended a model where the funds will be rolled out based on
  annual approval. He recommended a commitment for one year with quarterly
  updates back to the city. He requested numerical metrics and key performance
  indicators (KPIs).

  Councilmember Silverstein shared a concern regarding hiring an athletics director
  who knows they have a job in the long term. He recommended committing to
  funding the first step of this project, which would be the $25,000 needed for the
  consultant portion to have a more detailed proposal. He noted that $50,000 was
  given through the grants program ($25,000 per each school) to be used for the arts.
  He mentioned that not everyone in the city uses the school system and they are
  being asked to use the tax base of the city. He stated that when this item is proposed
  he would like to see a commitment from the council to explore other things we can
  be spending tax dollars on, that would benefit a portion of the population that does
  not benefit from the schools, such as a new senior center.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart shared that there are community pockets throughout
  Malibu, such as parks and the pool. He stated he is prepared to make a
  recommendation to the council to fund the first calendar year with quarterly reviews
  and subject to performance reviews.

  Councilmember Silverstein proposed funding per school year as opposed to
  calendar year.

  Ms. Al-Hardan clarified that the first two quarters in the budget sheet are reflective
  of the second half of the 2023-2024 school year and the second two quarters are the
  first half of the 2024-2025 school year. She also mentioned that the athletic
  coordinator for Santa Monica is hired on an annual basis.

  Councilmember Silverstein indicated support for providing the money necessary
  for a consultant, money to get the athletics program running, work through the
  beginning of next year, and funding the arts. He stated he would want to see another
  presentation in July for a proposal to fund the school year.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart reviewed the proposed recommended commitments which
  would be $22,000 for the consultant, $175,000 for the arts and instructional aids,
  and the first three rows of the budget sheet for athletics, and a portion of the fourth
  row for the athletics coordinator. He requested comments from city staff.

  City Manager McClary stated that if this recommendation from the subcommittee
  was supported by the City Council, staff would incorporate these funds as part of
  the mid-year budget adjustment which would fund through the end of June 2024.
  He shared that if the City Council desired, the funds could be programmed as a

  placeholder through the budget discussions with the caveat of having an annual
  approval in future budget years. He agreed with Councilmember Silverstein that
  the proposal is premature and would like to hear a little bit more. He cautioned that
  there is 200k in the general fund grant program and he understands that the
  committee and the City Council struggle with trying to allocate and balance out all
  the requests. He reminded the committee to keep that in mind as they consider this
  request, stated that it may be harder to say no in the future to other requests. He
  shared that at the staff level they could reach out to the grant consultant to see if
  they had ideas that may assist in this effort.

  Councilmember Silverstein requested more information on how much the City of
  Santa Monica funded to get the Santa Monica Education Foundation up and running
  and what the numbers are for the other Las Virgenes-Malibu Council of
  Governments cities.

  Assistant City Manager Toney echoed City Manager McClary’s statement and
  cautioned against funding special interest items because this will set a new
  precedent for future requests made outside of the budget process. He stated that this
  request has not been vetted by city staff. He shared that this could be a larger project
  long term that has not been considered as part of the strategic priorities. He shared
  that they could figure it out and come up with strategies but there is still some
  sticker shock to the high price tag.

  Ms. Al-Hardan shared that she appreciates the feedback and mentioned that
  according to the last Census 20% of the population is under 18 and  about
  1000 of them go to Malibu schools.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart reopened public comment.

  Joe Drummond spoke in favor of the city helping fund the schools through this
  project.

  Mayor Pro Tem Stewart closed public comment.

  Assistant City Manager Toney stated that this would need to be reviewed by the
  City Attorney’s office and would likely need an MOU in place.

  Ms. Al-Hardan shared that the already established Shark Fund could potentially
  serve as a temporary solution while they work with the consultant to get established.

Subject:  Funding for City Owned Vacant Lot Outreach & Education

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Provide a recommendation to the City Council on
appropriation of an additional $55,000 from the General Fund Undesignated Reserve for
City Owned Vacant Lot Outreach and Education.

FISCAL IMPACT: Not to exceed $130,000, the Public Works Engineering – Professional
Services budget was approved by the City Council on June 21, 2023, includes the cost to
hire a firm to conduct outreach and education related to city-owned vacant lots in the City
of Malibu. Initial funding for this project is included in the Adopted Budget for FY 2023-24
in Account No. 100-3008-5100 (Professional Services) in the amount of $75,000 (see pg.
114 of approved budget). The additional appropriation of $55,000 will provide a total of
$130,000 for the selected firm to perform the services defined in the scope of work.

The General Fund Undesignated Reserve as of June 30, 2023, is $70.3 million.

WORK PLAN:  This item supports the Master Plan for City Owned Vacant Lots priority
identified in the Adopted FY 2023-24 Strategic Priority Project List.

DISCUSSION:  At the September 27, 2023, City Council meeting, the City Council
approved the City’s first Strategic Plan list to help focus and prioritize staff efforts on the
most important projects that City staff need to work on. As part of that plan, the City Council
identified the need for a comprehensive outreach and education program to engage the
Malibu community and stakeholders regarding vacant lots owned by the City.

  Page 1 of 2

 The City initiated a competitive RFP process on October 5, 2024, to identify a qualified
consultant for the project. Nine proposals were received, and after a detailed evaluation,
four consultants were invited to participate in interviews. The proposed consultant
emerged as the preferred choice based on their expertise, experience, innovative
approach, and understanding of the project’s objectives.

The initial budget for the professional services related to this project was estimated at
$75,000. However, after careful review and discussions among staff, it was determined
that an additional appropriation of $55,000 is necessary to ensure the successful
implementation of the outreach and education initiatives. The recommended not-to-
exceed amount of $130,000 has been deemed sufficient to accomplish the project’s
deliverables while ensuring fiscal responsibility.

Subject:  FY 2022-23 Fourth Quarter Financial Report

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Review FY 2022-23 Fourth Quarter financial information.

FISCAL IMPACT: As of June 30, 2023, the budget General Fund Undesignated Reserve
at June 30, 2023, is $70.3 million.

DISCUSSION: The attached report provides revenue, expenditure, and fund balance
totals for the fourth quarter of FY 2022-23.

The Adopted Budget is approved by City Council, typically in June, via resolution, and the
Amended Budget includes the ongoing appropriation revisions that occur throughout the
fiscal year, including the Mid-Year Budget Adjustments.

Revenues
As the Revenues by Fund Report (pages A 1-5) shows, the General Fund revenues have
exceeded budget estimates. Specifically, the report reflects General Fund revenues
received of $55.02 million or 101.0% of the amended budget amount and 118.0% of the
adopted budget for the fiscal year. The General Fund revenue sources were
conservatively budgeted, as is the best practice, and were based on review of information
available from the State and County. Total revenue of all funds received during the fiscal
year is $67.43 million or 72.0% of the amended budgeted amount for the fiscal year.

Many of the City’s tax revenues outperformed the projected budget. Property Tax
revenues overall came in at $17.86 million, which is $352,000 more than the amended
budget amount. The City received $3.06 million in Utility User’s Tax which is $858,000
  Page 1 of 3

 more than the amended budget. Most of the revenues came in at budget, or close to it, of
what was projected and amended as part of the FY 2022-23 Mid-Year Budget.

Transient Occupancy Tax (TOT) – Hotels and Motels and Private Rentals, collectively,
came in at the Amended Budget amount of $9.50 million. This is less than the $10.34
million the City received in the prior fiscal year, likely due to a regression from the spike of
demand in FY 2021-22 coming out of the pandemic. The $9 million to $10 million range is
likely the basis of TOT revenue going forward.

Licenses and Permits - Building and renovations in the community continue to be active
as Planning, Environmental Sustainability, and Public Works are still experiencing a
greater-than-average number of applications, reviewing projects, and processing permits.
Revenue from Licenses and Permits ($4.13 million) exceeded the adopted budget ($3.52
million) by nearly $611,000, and $223,000 over the amended budget ($3.91 million).

Service Charges - Revenue from Service Charges of $4.96 million resulted in more than
the adopted budget ($4.7 million) by $260,000, but shortfall from the amended budget
($5.76 million) of -$806,000. The amended budget shortfall is due primarily to permits/fees
being generated less than projected at Mid-Year for Dark Sky, Building Plan Check, and
Geo Soils Engineering.

Overall, the total General Fund Revenues of $55.02 million resulted in $528,000 more
than the amended budget ($54.49 million) and $8.83 million more than was anticipated at
adoption ($46.19 million).

Expenditures
The Expenditure by Fund Report (pages A 6-9) reflects any budget carryovers from FY
2021-22, as well as the appropriations approved by the City Council for the current fiscal
year in the Amended Budget column. Budget Adjustments, Carryovers and Council
Appropriations total $3.68 million as of June 30, 2023. General Fund expenditures for the
fiscal year total $40.41 million or 84.5% of the amended budgeted amount. Expenditures
for all funds total $52.4 million or 56.1% of the amended budgeted amount. The low
expenditure amount of all funds in relation to the budget is primarily due to pauses in
progress on capital projects, the most significant of which is the $16.5 million for the Civic
Center Water Treatment Facility (CCWTF) Phase Two. In addition, staffing vacancies are
the main reason for savings across the departments.

Fund Balances
Projected Fund Balances for the fiscal year end are reflected on page A-10. The
Undesignated Fund Balance at June 30, 2023, reflects all expenses appropriated by the
Council as of June 30, 2023. The City ended FY 2021-22 with $56.45 million in the
Undesignated General Fund Reserve. As of June 30, 2023, the budget General Fund
Undesignated Reserve is $70.30 million, this will be approximately 120.9% of the $58.17

Revenues
The Revenues by Fund Report (pages A-1 through A-5) reflects General Fund revenues
received of $21.3 million or 37% of the amended budgeted amount for the fiscal year. Total
revenue for all funds received through the second quarter is $25.65 million or 31.1% of
the Amended Budget amount for the fiscal year. Many revenue sources are received on a
quarterly or annual basis and, as such, will be reflected when the year-end report is
presented. For example, property taxes are remitted by the County after they are paid by
property owners in December and April; Property Tax - In Lieu payments typically come
at the end of the year; and Transient Occupancy Tax - Private Rentals is remitted quarterly.
Therefore, this report only reflects payments made in October for the period of July through
September. The second quarter payments will be received by the end of January and are
not included in this report. Sales Tax is remitted quarterly to the State and then passed
along to the City, so there is some lag in those receipts as well. Additionally, total City
revenue includes grant reimbursements for Capital Improvement Projects (CIP)
expenditures that are typically received at the end of the fiscal year.

Expenditures
The Expenditure by Fund Report (pages A-6 through A-9) reflects budget carryovers from
FY 2022-23, as well as the appropriations approved by the City Council for the current
fiscal year in the Amended Budget column. Budget Adjustments, Carryovers, Corrections
and Council Appropriations total $2,035,817 through December 31, 2023. General Fund
expenditures for the second quarter total $19.95 million or 28.3% of the Amended Budget
amount. Reducing for the General Fund CIP and Disaster Response amounts, the total is
$19.93 million or 35.7% of the Amended Budget. Expenditures for all funds total $25.0
million or 26.3% of the Amended Budget amount.

Undesignated Fund Balance at June 30, 2024, includes all expenses appropriated by the

Personnel
The Community Services Department is requesting to transition four part-time positions
into permanent part-time, thus providing benefits. The intent is to improve retention of
seasonal staff, which has been growing more and more difficult to recruit and retain. The
change is expected to be neutral on the FTE count as the hours worked per post for CSD
programs will remain the same. The number of staff required to fill those posts will be
reduced to permanent staff members, requiring less recruitment and seasonal hires. The
estimated impact of this change is $200,000, included as an amendment in this report.

The change will require the Council to adopt an updated Salary Resolution for FY 2023-
24. The resolution will be included with the Mid-Year Report to Council.

 Anticipated Future Revenue Impacts
The City’s revenues have continued to see steady growth in the major tax revenue
categories post-pandemic and are anticipated to continue to grow in the major tax revenue
categories. The voter-approved Transactions and Use Tax (TUT) went into effect on April
1, 2023, and was estimated to bring in $3.0 million per year. The current projection for FY
2023-24 is $3.6 million.

Anticipated Unfunded Expenditures
The Sheriff substation was intended to be open during FY 2023-24, but has yet to open
primarily due to Sheriff staffing shortages. While this was originally thought to be a
potential fiscal issue, the current status has created expenditure savings. Nevertheless,
the ongoing efforts to improve Pacific Coast Highway safety could have significant
financial impacts.

The State of California released the budget proposal on January 10, 2024, initially
projecting a $38 billion deficit. Furthermore, the Federal Reserve continues to strive for a
“soft landing” on the economy. These headwinds could signal economic turbulence in the
future, and staff will monitor if any impacts will be felt at the local level.

The FY 2023-24 Second Quarter Mid-Year Financial Report and Salary Resolution will be
presented to the City Council on February 12, 2024.
